mainTopic: Humility (רבי אלעזר and the ugly man), the laws of fasting for collapsing walls, and the merits and good deeds of רב אדא בר אהבה and רב הונא.
overview: The עמוד opens by finishing the story of רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון, who insulted a very ugly man. The man told him to complain to the Craftsman who made him, and forgave him only after the townspeople pleaded. רבי אלעזר then taught that a person should be soft like a reed, not stiff like a cedar. The גמרא returns to the משנה about fasting for collapsing buildings. A ברייתא explains that only sturdy walls falling counts, not walls already likely to fall, such as very tall walls or walls on a riverbank. Stories follow about a weak wall and the protective merit of רב אדא בר אהבה, together with רבי ינאי's warning never to rely on a miracle. רב אדא בר אהבה then lists the habits that earned him long life. Finally, רפרם בר פפא describes the kind deeds of רב הונא, and רבא says he can follow all of them but one, which the next עמוד explains.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר insults an ugly man
steps.stepSummary: An extremely ugly man greets רבי אלעזר politely. רבי אלעזר does not answer the greeting and insults his looks instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: He met a man who was extremely ugly. The man said, 'Peace upon you, רבי!' He did not answer him. Instead he said, 'Empty one, how ugly that man is! Are all the people of your town as ugly as you?'
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: רבי אלעזר, feeling proud, meets an ugly man and insults him instead of returning his greeting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man was the respectful one: he greeted first and called him 'רבי.' רבי אלעזר answered with an insult about something the man could not control, his appearance. This sets up the lesson about arrogance that the story builds toward.

phrases.english: A certain man happened to meet him
who was extremely ugly.
He said to him: Peace upon you, my teacher!
But he did not return his greeting.
He said to him: Empty one,
how ugly is that man!
phrases.notes: A polite way of saying 'how ugly you are.'

phrases.english: Perhaps all the people of your town
are as ugly as you?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story begun on the previous עמוד of רבי אלעזר returning proudly from his teacher's house.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative: רבי אלעזר insults a man for his looks.

steps.title: The man answers: go complain to my Maker
steps.stepSummary: The man answers that he does not know. If רבי אלעזר has a complaint, he should take it to the Craftsman who made him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: I don't know. But go and say to the Craftsman who made me, 'How ugly is this vessel that You made.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ugly man gives a sharp reply that points the insult back at ה׳, his Creator.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man's point is that mocking someone's looks is really criticizing ה׳'s handiwork. He calls himself a 'vessel' and ה׳ the 'Craftsman.' This one line makes רבי אלעזר realize his mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: vessel, utensil (the man calls himself this)

phrases.english: He said to him: I do not know,
but go and say to the Craftsman who made me:
'How ugly is this vessel that You made.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The man's response to the insult in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Insulting a person's appearance is like insulting the Creator.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר begs forgiveness and is refused
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר realizes he sinned. He gets off his donkey, bows down, and asks forgiveness. The man refuses unless he goes and tells the Craftsman that His vessel is ugly.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he realized that he had sinned, he got off the donkey, bowed down before him, and said, 'I have wronged you, forgive me!' The man said, 'I will not forgive you until you go to the Craftsman who made me and say: How ugly is this vessel that You made.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר does תשובה right away and humbles himself, but the man refuses to forgive him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Getting down from the donkey shows he is lowering himself after his pride. The man's refusal is a way of saying, 'You can't undo this.' Nobody would dare say such a thing to ה׳, so the insult was truly serious.

keyTerms.meaning: I have wronged you / I submit to you

phrases.english: Once he realized in himself that he had sinned,
he got down from the donkey and bowed down before him,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר לוֹ: נַעֲנֵיתִי לְךָ, מְחוֹל לִי!
phrases.english: and said to him: I have wronged you, forgive me!
He said to him: I will not forgive you
until you go to the Craftsman who made me

phrases.aramaic: וֶאֱמוֹר לוֹ: כַּמָּה מְכוֹעָר כְּלִי זֶה שֶׁעָשִׂיתָ.
phrases.english: and say to Him: How ugly is this vessel that You made.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי אלעזר reacts to the man's reply with regret.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative: immediate regret and a request for forgiveness, which is refused.

steps.title: The townspeople greet רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר follows the man all the way to his own town. The townspeople come out and greet him with great honor.
steps.simpleTranslation: He walked behind him until he reached his town. The people of his town came out to meet him and said, 'Peace upon you, רבי, רבי! My master, my master!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר keeps following the man to win his forgiveness. Now the townspeople's honor sets up the next dialogue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The great scholar now walks behind the simple man, which is a full reversal of his earlier pride. The townspeople's honor reveals to the ugly man who he really insulted.

phrases.english: He was walking behind him
until he reached his town.
The people of his town came out to greet him,
and they were saying to him:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלוֹם עָלֶיךָ רַבִּי רַבִּי, מוֹרִי מוֹרִי!
phrases.english: Peace upon you, my teacher, my teacher, my master, my master!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה מְטַיֵּיל אַחֲרָיו עַד שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְעִירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After being refused, רבי אלעזר keeps trying to make peace.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative setup for the townspeople's involvement.

steps.title: The man says: may there not be many like him
steps.stepSummary: The man asks who they are calling 'רבי.' When he hears it is the one following him, he says Israel should not have many like him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them, 'Whom are you calling רבי, רבי?' They said, 'This man who is walking behind you.' He said, 'If this is a רבי, may there not be many like him in Israel!'
steps.whatsHappening: The ugly man learns who רבי אלעזר is and openly criticizes him in front of his own townspeople.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His point is that a real Torah teacher should never act this way. The criticism is about מידות, good character, and not about Torah knowledge.

keyTerms.meaning: may there not be many like him

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: לְמִי אַתֶּם קוֹרִין רַבִּי רַבִּי?
phrases.english: He said to them: Whom are you calling 'my teacher, my teacher'?
They said to him: This one who is walking behind you.
He said to them: If this is a teacher,
may there not be many like him in Israel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The man reacts to the townspeople's greeting.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative: a scholar with bad character is not a model to be multiplied.

steps.title: The townspeople plead for forgiveness
steps.stepSummary: The townspeople ask why he said that. He tells them what happened, and they ask him to forgive רבי אלעזר anyway because he is great in Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said, 'Why?' He said, 'He did such and such to me.' They said, 'Even so, forgive him, because he is a man great in Torah.'
steps.whatsHappening: The townspeople step in and ask the man to forgive רבי אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They do not defend what רבי אלעזר did. They admit it was wrong ('even so') but ask for forgiveness out of respect for his Torah greatness. This is what finally moves the man.

phrases.english: They said to him: For what reason?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: כָּךְ וְכָךְ עָשָׂה לִי.
phrases.english: He said to them: He did such and such to me.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אַף עַל פִּי כֵּן, מְחוֹל לוֹ,
phrases.english: They said to him: Even so, forgive him,
for he is a man great in Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל פִּי כֵּן, מְחוֹל לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The townspeople ask about the man's criticism and then plead for רבי אלעזר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative: a request to forgive because of כבוד התורה.

steps.title: The man forgives, with a condition
steps.stepSummary: The man forgives for the sake of the townspeople. His condition is that רבי אלעזר must not make a habit of acting this way.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them, 'For your sake I forgive him, as long as he does not get used to doing this.'
steps.whatsHappening: The conflict is resolved: the man grants forgiveness on one condition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The forgiveness comes because the community asked, not because of רבי אלעזר's own request. The condition shows that real forgiveness goes together with a commitment not to repeat the wrong.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: בִּשְׁבִילְכֶם הֲרֵינִי מוֹחֵל לוֹ,
phrases.english: He said to them: For your sake I hereby forgive him,

phrases.aramaic: וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא רָגִיל לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן.
phrases.english: provided that he does not become accustomed to doing this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The man responds to the townspeople's plea.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Forgiveness is granted on condition that the behavior is not repeated.

steps.title: Be soft like a reed, not stiff like a cedar
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר immediately teaches the lesson he learned. A person should be flexible like a reed, not rigid like a cedar. That is why the reed was chosen to make the quill for writing a ספר תורה, תפילין, and מזוזות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Right away רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון went in and taught: A person should always be soft like a reed and not hard like a cedar. That is why the reed merited to have a quill made from it to write a ספר תורה, תפילין, and מזוזות.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with its moral: רבי אלעזר publicly teaches humility based on what just happened to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A reed bends with the wind and survives, while a stiff cedar can break. A soft, humble person is like the reed. Because of its humility the reed became the tool for writing holy texts, so humility brings a person closer to תורה, not further from it.
steps.whatToRemember: The whole story teaches one point: Torah learning must lead to humility. Being 'soft like a reed' is what makes a person fit to carry Torah.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a famous source for the מידה of ענווה, humility, and for being careful never to shame another person.

phrases.aramaic: מִיָּד נִכְנַס רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, וְדָרַשׁ:
phrases.english: Immediately Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon entered and expounded:
A person should always be soft like a reed
and not be hard like a cedar.
And therefore the reed merited
to have a quill taken from it

phrases.aramaic: לִכְתּוֹב בּוֹ סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה תְּפִילִּין וּמְזוּזוֹת.
phrases.english: to write with it a Torah scroll, tefillin, and mezuzot.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם יְהֵא אָדָם רַךְ כְּקָנֶה וְאַל יְהֵא קָשֶׁה כְּאֶרֶז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the moral from the whole story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Be humble and flexible like a reed, which merited to become the pen for writing holy texts.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: a city with plague or collapses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה, which says a city struck by plague or collapsing buildings fasts and sounds the alarm.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The משנה said:] And likewise, a city that has plague or collapsing buildings, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The story is over. The גמרא now quotes the next line of the משנה to set up its explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'כו׳' means 'etc.': the rest of the משנה is assumed. It says that city fasts and sounds the alarm, and its neighbors fast but do not sound the alarm. The next step will define what kind of 'collapse' counts.
steps.confusionAlert: The topic changes sharply here. The story is finished, and we are now back to the laws of public fasts from the משנה.

phrases.english: And likewise, a city in which there is
plague or collapsing buildings, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן עִיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ דֶּבֶר אוֹ מַפּוֹלֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story and returns to the משנה text.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A city struck by plague or building collapses fasts and sounds the alarm.

steps.title: Which collapses count: only sturdy walls
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that the 'collapse' in the משנה means sturdy walls that fall, not weak walls that were already ready to fall.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: The 'collapse' they spoke of means sturdy walls, not shaky ones. Walls that were not expected to fall, and not walls that were expected to fall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to define the word מפולת in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a weak, cracked wall falls, that is normal and not a sign of Heavenly anger. When strong walls fall without reason, it shows a real calamity, which calls for a fast and an alarm.
steps.whatToRemember: A fast for מפולת is declared only when sturdy walls collapse. Weak walls falling is natural and does not count.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: The collapse that they spoke of
means sturdy walls and not shaky ones.
Walls that are not expected to fall,
and not those that are expected to fall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the term מפולת from the משנה quoted in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only the collapse of sturdy walls counts as a calamity that requires a fast.

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to repeat itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how 'sound' walls are different from walls 'not ready to fall,' and how 'dilapidated' walls are different from walls 'ready to fall.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What are 'sound' walls? They are the same as walls that are not ready to fall! What are 'dilapidated' walls? They are the same as walls that are ready to fall!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the wording of the ברייתא from step 10. It says the ברייתא uses two pairs of words that mean the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said the משנה means sturdy walls that are 'not ready to fall,' and not weak walls that are 'ready to fall.' The גמרא argues that 'sturdy' already means 'not ready to fall,' so the ברייתא seems to say the same thing twice. The גמרא needs to find a case where a wall is sturdy but still ready to fall.

keyTerms.meaning: Which is it? / What exactly is meant?

phrases.english: What are 'sound' walls?
They are the same as walls that are not ready to fall.
What are 'dilapidated' walls?
They are the same as walls that are ready to fall!
phrases.notes: The exclamation shows this is a challenge: the wording looks repetitive.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵי נִיהוּ בְּרִיאוֹת, הֵי נִיהוּ שֶׁאֵינָן רְאוּיוֹת לִיפּוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the ברייתא quoted in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The double description in the ברייתא: 'sound / not ready to fall' and 'dilapidated / ready to fall.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The paired terms look like synonyms, so the ברייתא seems to repeat itself for no reason.

steps.title: Strong walls that fall because they are too tall
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is needed for strong walls that fell only because they were very tall.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the ברייתא is needed for walls that fell because of their height.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by giving a case where a wall is strong but still likely to fall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A very tall wall can be well built and still unstable because of its height. Such a wall is 'sound' but also 'ready to fall.' The ברייתא teaches that when walls like this fall, it does not count as the unusual disaster the משנה describes.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a specific case)

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
for walls that fell because of their height.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case limitation: shows a case where the two terms do not overlap.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed 'sound' always means 'not ready to fall.'
steps.terutzMaskana: A sound wall can still be ready to fall because of its great height.

steps.title: Second answer: walls on a riverbank
steps.stepSummary: Another case of a strong wall that is ready to fall is a wall standing on a riverbank.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or else, the ברייתא is talking about walls that stand on the bank of a river.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, alternative answer to the same challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wall on a riverbank may be built well, but the ground under it is weak and can wash away. So it is 'sound' in its building but still 'ready to fall.' Either example explains why the ברייתא needed both descriptions.

keyTerms.meaning: On the bank of a river

phrases.english: Alternatively, where they stand on the bank of a river.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer, next to step 12's answer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A well-built wall should not be at risk.
steps.terutzMaskana: Unstable ground, like a riverbank, makes even a well-built wall ready to fall.
steps.whatToRemember: A 'collapse' that requires a fast means strong walls falling for no normal reason. Walls that were already at risk, whether because they are weak, very tall, or on a riverbank, do not count.

steps.title: The dangerous wall in נהרדעא
steps.stepSummary: There was a weak wall in נהרדעא that רב and שמואל would not walk under, even though it had stood for thirteen years.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like that weak wall in נהרדעא. רב and שמואל would not pass under it, even though it had stood in its place for thirteen years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from the law of 'ready to fall' walls to a story about one such wall. This opens a series of stories.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the wall had lasted thirteen years, רב and שמואל still treated it as dangerous and avoided it. This shows that a weak wall stays 'ready to fall' no matter how long it has stood. It sets up the next part of the story.

keyTerms.meaning: נהרדעא, a Babylonian city where שמואל lived

phrases.english: Like that dilapidated wall
that was in Nehardea,

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא הֲוָה חָלֵיף רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל תּוּתַהּ,
phrases.english: under which Rav and Shmuel would not pass,
even though it stood in its place
thirteen years.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הַהִיא אֲשִׁיתָא רְעִיעֲתָא דַּהֲוַאי בִּנְהַרְדְּעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life example of a wall that is 'ready to fall.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A weak wall is treated as dangerous even if it has stood for many years.

steps.title: רב relies on רב אדא בר אהבה's merit
steps.stepSummary: When רב אדא בר אהבה was with them, רב said there was no need to walk around the wall, because his merit protected them.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day רב אדא בר אהבה came there. שמואל said to רב: 'Come, let us go around the wall.' רב answered: 'We do not need to today. רב אדא בר אהבה is with us, and his merit is great, so I am not afraid.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. רב feels safe walking near the dangerous wall because a great צדיק is with them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally רב and שמואל avoided the wall. Here רב says the great merit (זכות) of רב אדא בר אהבה protects everyone with him. This introduces the main theme of the next stories: the protective merit of רב אדא בר אהבה.

phrases.english: One day there happened to come
Rav Adda bar Ahava, to there.
Shmuel said to Rav:
Come, Master, let us go around!
He said to him: We do not need to now,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִיכָּא רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה בַּהֲדַן
phrases.english: because Rav Adda bar Ahava is with us,
whose merit is great,
and I am not afraid.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹמָא חַד אִיקְּלַע רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה לְהָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of the wall in נהרדעא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The great merit of a צדיק can protect the people who are with him.

steps.title: רב הונא uses רב אדא בר אהבה's presence to save his wine
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא had wine in a weak house. He brought רב אדא בר אהבה inside and kept him busy with Torah learning until all the wine was moved out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא had some wine in a certain weak house, and he wanted to move it out. He brought רב אדא בר אהבה there and kept him busy with a Torah discussion until the wine was all moved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story about the merit of רב אדא בר אהבה. This time someone used that merit without telling him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא was afraid the house would fall while the wine was being moved. He relied on רב אדא בר אהבה's merit and kept him there by stretching out a הלכה discussion. The point is that רב אדא בר אהבה did not know he was being used for protection.

keyTerms.meaning: To clear it out / remove it
A Torah teaching / discussion of הלכה

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ הָהוּא חַמְרָא
phrases.english: Rav Huna had a certain amount of wine
in a certain dilapidated house,
and he wanted to remove it.

phrases.aramaic: עַיְּילֵיהּ לְרַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה לְהָתָם,
phrases.english: He brought Rav Adda bar Ahava in there,
he drew him out in a halachic discussion
until they had removed it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ הָהוּא חַמְרָא בְּהָהוּא בֵּיתָא רְעִיעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story showing the protective merit of רב אדא בר אהבה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא relied on רב אדא בר אהבה's merit to protect the work in the dangerous house.

steps.title: The house falls and רב אדא בר אהבה is upset
steps.stepSummary: Right after they left, the house fell down. רב אדא בר אהבה realized what had happened and became upset.
steps.simpleTranslation: After he went out, the house fell. רב אדא בר אהבה understood what had happened, and he was upset.
steps.whatsHappening: The story reaches its surprising ending. רב אדא בר אהבה is angry, and this sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The house falling right after they left proves it was his merit that held it up. But instead of being pleased, he was upset. The reader is left asking why, and the next step gives the answer.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think he was upset because the house fell or because the wine was saved. He was upset that his merit was used up on a miracle without his agreement, as the next step explains.

phrases.english: After he went out, the house fell.
Rav Adda bar Ahava realized what had happened,
and he became angry.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the רב הונא story and raises the question of why he was upset.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב אדא בר אהבה was upset that his merit was relied on for a miracle.

steps.title: Why he was upset: never rely on a miracle
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה agreed with רבי ינאי: do not put yourself in danger and expect a miracle. A miracle might not happen, and if it does, it is taken away from your merits.
steps.simpleTranslation: He held like רבי ינאי, who said: A person should never stand in a dangerous place and say, 'A miracle will be done for me,' because maybe no miracle will be done for him. And even if a miracle is done for him, it is taken away from his merits.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב אדא בר אהבה was angry by quoting a teaching of רבי ינאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two problems with relying on a miracle. First, it might not come, and you will be hurt. Second, even if it comes, it uses up some of your merits (זכויות). רב הונא's plan used up רב אדא בר אהבה's merits without asking him, so he was upset.

keyTerms.meaning: It is deducted from his merits

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known principle in הלכה and השקפה: a person may not put himself in danger and count on a miracle (אין סומכין על הנס).

phrases.english: He holds like this teaching
that Rabbi Yannai said:

phrases.aramaic: לְעוֹלָם אַל יַעֲמוֹד אָדָם בְּמָקוֹם סַכָּנָה
phrases.english: A person should never stand in a place of danger
and say: A miracle will be done for me,
because perhaps a miracle will not be done for him.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר עוֹשִׂין לוֹ נֵס —
phrases.english: And even if you say a miracle is done for him,
it is deducted from his merits.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבַר לַהּ כִּי הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason for רב אדא בר אהבה's anger in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Never rely on a miracle in a dangerous place. It may not happen, and if it does, it reduces your merits.

steps.title: The verse behind the teaching: יעקב's words
steps.stepSummary: רב חנן brings a verse from יעקב: 'I have become small from all the kindnesses,' showing that kindness from ה׳ reduces a person's merits.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנן said: What verse hints to this? As it is written: 'I have become small from all the kindnesses and from all the truth.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חנן gives a source in the תורה for רבי ינאי's idea that miracles use up a person's merits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before meeting עשו, יעקב said 'קטנתי' — 'I have become small' because of all the kindness ה׳ had already done for him. This means the kindnesses made his merits smaller. That supports רבי ינאי's teaching that a miracle is deducted from one's merits.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the verse (that supports this)?

steps.whatToRemember: The stories of רב אדא בר אהבה teach that a צדיק's merit can protect people, but relying on miracles has a cost: it uses up merit. As יעקב said, 'קטנתי מכל החסדים.'

phrases.english: Rav Chanan said: What is the verse?
As it is written: 'I have become small from all the kindnesses'
'and from all the truth.'
phrases.notes: בראשית לב:יא — יעקב's prayer before meeting עשו.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a verse to support רבי ינאי's teaching in step 18.
steps.raayaObject: רבי ינאי's teaching that a miracle is deducted from a person's merits.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית לב:יא — 'קטנתי מכל החסדים ומכל האמת.'

steps.title: What did רב אדא בר אהבה do to earn his merit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what special deeds gave רב אדא בר אהבה such great merit.
steps.simpleTranslation: What were the special deeds of רב אדא בר אהבה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא just told us that רב אדא בר אהבה's merit was so great that people were protected because of him. Now it asks what he did to earn that merit, and this sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier we saw that his זכות protected a whole group and that a house did not fall while he was inside. The natural follow-up is to ask which actions built up so much merit. The question opens a new section about how he lived.

phrases.english: What were the deeds
of Rav Adda bar Ahava?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the stories of his merit by asking where that merit came from.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which deeds of רב אדא בר אהבה earned him his great merit.

steps.title: His students ask how he lived so long, and he starts his list
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with a teaching in which רב אדא בר אהבה's students asked him the reason for his long life. He begins to list his good habits.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: his students asked רב אדא בר אהבה, 'How did you earn a long life?' He told them: 'In all my days I never got angry inside my home, and I never walked in front of someone greater than me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by quoting a teaching. In it, רב אדא בר אהבה tells his students which habits earned him a long life, and he starts with two of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase כי הא דאתמר tells us the answer comes from a teaching that already exists. His first two habits are about how he treated people: he stayed calm with his family and showed honor to greater people. The list continues in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: as it was taught (quoting a known teaching)
I got angry or was strict

phrases.english: As it was stated:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאֲלוּ תַּלְמִידָיו לְרַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה:
phrases.english: His students asked Rav Adda bar Ahava:
Through what did you merit a long life?
He said to them:
In all my days I never got angry inside my home,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא צָעַדְתִּי בִּפְנֵי מִי שֶׁגָּדוֹל מִמֶּנִּי,
phrases.english: and I never walked in front of someone greater than me,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: His merit came from a list of careful habits, starting with not getting angry at home and honoring greater people.

steps.title: The rest of רב אדא בר אהבה's good habits
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה finishes his list: he respected Torah and תפילין, never slept in the בית המדרש, never enjoyed a friend's failure, and never called a friend by an insulting name.
steps.simpleTranslation: I never thought about Torah in dirty alleys. I never walked four אמות without Torah and without תפילין. I never slept in the בית המדרש, not a long sleep and not a short nap. I never was happy when a friend failed. I never called a friend by his nickname, and some say: by his insulting family name.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר אהבה continues and finishes his list of habits. These are about honoring Torah and treating friends kindly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some habits show honor for Torah: no Torah thoughts in filthy places, always having Torah and תפילין, and no sleeping in the בית המדרש. The others show care for friends: no joy at their failures and no hurtful names. ואמרי לה brings a second version of the last habit.

keyTerms.meaning: his nickname or his insulting family name

steps.whatToRemember: רב אדא בר אהבה's merit came from small daily habits: honoring Torah, honoring people, and never embarrassing a friend.
steps.confusionAlert: ואמרי לה is not a new habit. It is another version of the same last habit about how not to call a friend.

phrases.english: and I did not think about Torah in dirty alleys,
and I did not walk four cubits
without Torah and without tefillin,
and I did not sleep in the study hall,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שֵׁינַת קֶבַע וְלֹא שֵׁינַת עֲרַאי,
phrases.english: not a real sleep and not a short nap,
and I was not happy at my friends' failures,
and I did not call my friend by his nickname,
and some say: by his insulting family name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the list of habits that began in step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Long life and merit come from honoring Torah and never shaming others.

steps.title: רבא asks about רב הונא's good deeds
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רפרם בר פפא to tell them about the fine deeds that רב הונא used to do.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רפרם בר פפא: Please tell us about some of the fine deeds that רב הונא used to do.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a second righteous person, רב הונא, who was mentioned earlier in the story with the weak house. רבא asks for his good deeds, and this sets up the stories that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works like the question about רב אדא בר אהבה, but now the focus is רב הונא. רבא asks רפרם בר פפא because he knew רב הונא personally. This opens a new short section.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַפְרָם בַּר פָּפָּא:
phrases.english: Rava said to Rafram bar Pappa:
Let the Master tell us
some of those fine deeds
that Rav Huna used to do!

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא לַן מָר מֵהָנֵי מִילֵּי מְעַלְּיָיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רב אדא בר אהבה's deeds to רב הונא's deeds.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What good deeds רב הונא did.

steps.title: רב הונא checked the city for weak walls
steps.stepSummary: רפרם בר פפא remembers רב הונא's old age. On cloudy days רב הונא toured the city and had weak walls knocked down. If the owner could not afford to rebuild, רב הונא paid for it himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: I don't remember his younger years, but I remember his old age. Every cloudy day they took him out in a golden carriage and he looked over the whole city. Any wall that was weak, he had knocked down. If the owner could pay, the owner rebuilt it. If not, רב הונא rebuilt it with his own money.
steps.whatsHappening: רפרם בר פפא answers רבא with a story. רב הונא protected people from weak walls that could fall in the rain, and he paid to rebuild them for people who could not afford it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On cloudy days rain might come and knock down weak walls onto people. רב הונא cared about safety, so he had those walls taken down before anyone got hurt. He also made sure poor owners would not lose their walls by paying for the rebuilding himself.
steps.whyThisMatters: This connects to the earlier theme of not staying near a dangerous wall or house. רב הונא actively removed such dangers for everyone.

phrases.english: He said to him:
His youth I do not remember,
his old age I remember.
For every cloudy day
they would take him out in a golden carriage,
and he would inspect the whole city.
And every wall that was weak,
he would have it knocked down.
If its owner was able, he rebuilt it,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לָא אֶפְשָׁר — בָּנֵי לַהּ אִיהוּ מִדִּידֵיהּ.
phrases.english: and if not, Rav Huna rebuilt it from his own money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's question from step 23 with a first good deed.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב הונא removed dangerous walls and paid to rebuild them for those who could not afford it.

steps.title: רב הונא bought leftover vegetables every Friday
steps.stepSummary: Every ערב שבת afternoon רב הונא sent a messenger to buy all the vegetables the sellers had left, and then threw them into the river.
steps.simpleTranslation: Every ערב שבת in the afternoon he sent a messenger to the market. He bought all the vegetables the gardeners had left over and threw them into the river.
steps.whatsHappening: רפרם בר פפא tells a second good deed of רב הונא. He bought the unsold vegetables so the sellers would not lose money before שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vegetables left unsold on ערב שבת would spoil, and the sellers would lose their money. רב הונא bought them all to protect the sellers. The surprising part is that he threw them away, and the גמרא will ask about that next.

phrases.english: And every Friday afternoon
he would send a messenger to the market,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֹל יַרְקָא דַּהֲוָה פָּיֵישׁ לְהוּ לְגִינָּאֵי,
phrases.english: and all the vegetables that were left over with the gardeners,
he would buy and throw into the river.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second good deed of רב הונא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא protected the sellers' income by buying their leftover produce.

steps.title: Why not give the vegetables to the poor?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב הונא threw the vegetables away instead of giving them to poor people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him give them to the poor!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the story. Throwing good food in the river looks wasteful when poor people could use it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the goal was kindness, giving the food to the poor would help two groups at once. So why waste it? The answer comes next.

phrases.english: But let him give them to the poor!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the choice to throw away the vegetables.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's throwing the vegetables into the river.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Giving the food to the poor seems like a better use than wasting it.

steps.title: The poor would stop buying from the sellers
steps.stepSummary: If he gave vegetables away, the poor would sometimes count on that and stop buying, which would hurt the sellers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sometimes they would rely on it and not come to buy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that giving the food to the poor would backfire. People would wait for free vegetables and stop buying from the sellers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole point was to protect the sellers' income. Free vegetables would cause fewer people to buy, so the sellers would end up with even more leftovers. Throwing the food away kept the market working normally.

phrases.english: Sometimes they would rely on it
and would not come to buy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains a hidden harm that the suggestion would cause.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Giving to the poor would help everyone.
steps.terutzMaskana: It would hurt the sellers, because the poor would stop buying.

steps.title: Why not feed the vegetables to animals?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב הונא did not at least give the vegetables to animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him throw them to the animals!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a second question. Even if he could not give the food to the poor, animals could eat it instead of it being wasted in the river.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Feeding animals would not hurt the sellers' business, so the first answer does not apply here. The גמרא wants to know why he still chose to throw the food away.

phrases.english: But let him throw them to the animals!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge that the answer of step 27 does not cover.
steps.kashyaTarget: Throwing the vegetables into the river.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Feeding animals avoids waste and does not hurt the sellers.

steps.title: Human food should not be fed to animals
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא held that food meant for people should not be given to animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: He held that human food may not be fed to an animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב הונא held a rule: food for people should not be given to animals, because that disrespects the food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קסבר shows this is רב הונא's own view of the הלכה. Giving human food to animals treats it with contempt. So the river was the only option left, which leads the גמרא to its next challenge in step 30.
steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא protected the sellers' income. He would not give the food to the poor, because that would hurt the sellers, and he would not feed it to animals, because human food should not go to animals.

phrases.english: He holds:
Human food may not be fed to an animal.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָסָבַר: מַאֲכַל אָדָם אֵין מַאֲכִילִין לִבְהֵמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a halachic principle רב הונא held.
steps.terutzMaskana: Feeding human food to animals is disrespectful, so he did not do it.

steps.title: Why buy the vegetables at all?
steps.stepSummary: If רב הונא could not use the vegetables for people or animals, why did he buy them in the first place?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then he should not buy them at all!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes one step further. If רב הונא ends up throwing the vegetables away, it looks pointless to buy them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 26–29 ruled out giving the vegetables to the poor and ruled out feeding them to animals. So the vegetables seem to have no use. If so, spending money on them seems wasteful.

phrases.english: But let him not buy it at all!
phrases.notes: A challenge based on the last two answers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the answer in step 29 to question the whole purchase.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's practice of buying all the leftover vegetables
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the vegetables cannot go to people or to animals, buying them seems like a waste of money.

steps.title: Leftovers would hurt future supply
steps.stepSummary: If the vegetables stayed unsold, the sellers would bring less next time, and people would lack vegetables for שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: You would be found to be causing them to stumble in the future.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the purchase protected the future market. Sellers who see unsold produce will bring less next week.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The goal was never to use the vegetables. The goal was to make sure the sellers felt it was worth bringing a full supply every ערב שבת. That way, people would always have enough for שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: You are found to be (you end up)
Causing them to stumble (causing them a loss)
In the future (here: in the coming weeks)

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא bought the leftovers so that the sellers would keep bringing enough for שבת. He threw them away because he would not hurt the sellers' business (step 27) and would not give human food to animals (step 29).
steps.confusionAlert: Here לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא does not mean the days of משיח. It simply means 'next time.'

phrases.english: You would be found causing them to stumble
in the future.
phrases.notes: Next week, the sellers would bring less produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the hidden purpose of the action
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Buying vegetables you will throw away is a waste.
steps.terutzMaskana: The purchase keeps the sellers bringing a full supply for future weeks.

steps.title: רב הונא's public medicine jug
steps.stepSummary: When רב הונא had a medicine, he filled a jug with it and hung it at his door for anyone to take.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he had a medicine, he would fill a jug with it, hang it at the doorway of his house, and say: Whoever needs, let him come and take.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now tells us another kind custom of רב הונא. He shared his medicines freely with the public.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new story, not a reply to the vegetable discussion. It adds to the picture of רב הונא as a man who cared for others.

phrases.english: When he had a medicine,
he would fill a jug (of water) [with it],
phrases.notes: The text has a correction: 'with it' (the medicine) replaces 'of water.'

phrases.english: and hang it at the doorway of the house,
and he would say: Whoever wants, let him come and take.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story in the list of רב הונא's customs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא made his medicines freely available to anyone who needed them.

steps.title: Another version: a water jug against שִׁבְתָּא
steps.stepSummary: Another version says רב הונא knew a remedy against the harmful spirit שִׁבְתָּא, so he hung a water jug by his door for people to wash their hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: He knew by tradition a remedy against שִׁבְתָּא. He would set out a water jug and hang it up, and say: Whoever needs, let him come in so that he will not be in danger.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the jug story. In this version, the jug held water for washing hands to protect against שִׁבְתָּא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two versions agree that רב הונא hung a jug by his door for the public. They disagree about what was inside: medicine, or water for protection from a harmful spirit.

keyTerms.meaning: A harmful spirit; washing hands protects against it

phrases.english: And some say:
He knew by tradition a remedy against שִׁבְתָּא,

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲוָה מַנַּח כּוּזָא דְמַיָּא וְדָלֵי לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: and he would set out a water jug and hang it up,
and he would say: Whoever needs,
let him come in (and wash), so that he will not be in danger.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of the story in step 32.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, רב הונא provided water for washing hands to protect people from שִׁבְתָּא.

steps.title: Open doors at mealtime
steps.stepSummary: When רב הונא sat down to eat bread, he opened his doors and invited anyone in need to come and eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he would eat bread, he would open his doors and say: Whoever needs, let him come and eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells one more of רב הונא's customs. He invited the hungry to join his meals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This custom goes further than the jug. Here רב הונא brings needy people into his own home to eat with him. This is the custom רבא will react to next.

phrases.english: When he would eat bread,
he would open his doors,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר: כׇּל מַאן דִּצְרִיךְ לֵיתֵי וְלֵיכוֹל.
phrases.english: and he would say: Whoever needs, let him come and eat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another custom to the list of רב הונא's kind deeds.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא invited anyone in need to eat at his table.

steps.title: רבא can copy all but one custom
steps.stepSummary: רבא says he can follow all of רב הונא's customs except one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: I can fulfill all of them, except for this one, which I cannot do.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא reacts to the list of רב הונא's customs. This line sets up the next move: the following passage will explain which custom רבא cannot do and why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא admires these customs and can follow most of them. He names one exception. Judging by the order, it is most likely the open-door meals, but the reason comes on the next עמוד.

phrases.english: רבא said:
All of them I am able to fulfill,
except for this one, which I am not able to do,
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next עמוד.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבא comments on the customs just listed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא can follow all of רב הונא's customs except one, which the next passage explains.
